name: Sara Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, parties or AI firms. Your answers stay confidential. Sara, what is a normal shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: At the yard I check the permit, ask an AI search to pull up the old fault notes, and then check the approved manual before we go out. Most of my day is climbing, fitting and testing line equipment. I love tracing a fault that everyone else walked past; I hate coming home to find a household bill we cannot absorb.

say: I would say **AI searches** help find fault records and approved drawings faster.
I would remind the crew that **wet conductor work** remains a human repair job.
think: I like the tool, but our **thin savings** make ordinary household surprises dangerous.
I cannot count on **storm overtime** to arrive before the mortgage payment.
do: Keep doing **line repairs** and show an apprentice how to verify manual pages.
Transfer **twenty per wage** to a separate emergency account starting next payday.
feel: I feel **confident at work** and exposed by our small cash cushion.
S0.quote: A small tool is pleasant; a leaking roof would still be a crisis.
fieldNote: Sara uses **AI daily** for manual searches and teaches an apprentice to verify results against approved pages.
Her work confidence contrasts with **household fragility**; a failed tap recently pushed groceries onto a card.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs and verify approved manual drawings
Show the apprentice how to check daily AI searches against approved pages
Transfer twenty from each wage payment into an emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew AI is handy for finding old fault reports, but it will not put a clamp on a wet conductor. I already use it each morning to search the manuals before we leave the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a quiet technology story still leaves us short of cash. Our savings would not cover a month, and the mortgage payment arrives whether a storm brings overtime or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep doing line repairs and show the apprentice how I check an AI search against the approved manual. From next payday, I would send twenty from each wage payment to a separate emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel confident about the craft and embarrassed by how little we have put away. A small tool is pleasant; a leaking roof would still be a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time a bill surprised you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kitchen tap failed in September and my partner bought the part while I was on call. We put groceries on a card until the next wage came in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why show the apprentice a tool you have to check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a search can find the right drawing quickly, and the approved page tells us whether the drawing is current. I would rather teach that distinction than pretend nobody uses a phone.

say: I would ask for a **field-tested plan** that orders the correct parts.
I would say crews should report **wrong orders** before targets or staffing change.
think: I expect **planners to shrink** before field repair crews, but dispatch errors could hurt our hours.
I want a useful pilot without **concealing mistakes** made by a smaller office team.
do: Volunteer for the paid **digital order pilot** and compare predicted parts with actual fittings.
Send the **error log** to the union safety representative during the first pilot year.
feel: I feel **curious** about better orders and concerned for office colleagues.
S1.quote: I would bring a real wrong-order example to the toolbox meeting instead of giving them a sales presentation.
fieldNote: Sara treats **field evidence** as the test of planning software and is eager to teach crews if repeat journeys fall.
She recognizes the possible **office job loss** and protects paid pilot time and safety reporting through her union representative.

steps.text: Test the digital work order pilot against actual pole fittings
Send logged order errors to the union safety representative
Keep taking paid line repairs during the pilot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that the new planning software should be tested by the people who open the cabinets. It could save a second trip if it orders the correct fuse, and we should record when it does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may lose some planners because writing and buying are easy to automate. Our hands are still needed, but a bad automated order could take a callout off our rota or delay a safe repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would volunteer for the next digital work order pilot and compare its parts list with what we find on site. In its first year I would send the error log to our union safety representative and ask that the pilot time stay paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested, then cautious when I think of the missing office colleagues. I want the useful part without making a smaller team hide its mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go in the error log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would include the pole number, the predicted fitting, the actual fitting and the extra journey. Last winter a mismatched fuse cost our van a second afternoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you teach other crews to use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the pilot shows fewer repeat journeys. I would bring a real wrong-order example to the toolbox meeting instead of giving them a sales presentation.

say: I would distinguish **2028 plans** from robots reaching live line repairs around 2031.
I would call for a **public trial log** before robots work near live wires.
think: I will be **48** at the robot date, and daily AI use does not protect my physical job.
A **wage gap** would be hard with children, a mortgage and less than one month saved.
do: Document **missed field faults** and seek company-paid inspection training now.
Keep **line shifts** after 2028 and apply for a funded inspection vacancy if it opens.
feel: I feel **rushed and alert**, with real fear of losing wages.
S2.quote: The three paid years matter, but my daily use of AI does not guarantee a job once machines can handle the physical repair too.
fieldNote: Sara understands the **robot lag** and treats continued paid repairs through 2028 as time to build evidence and options.
Her **daily AI fluency** does not erase the mortgage risk; she conditions any move on funded pay and clear field duties.

steps.text: Keep paid line repair shifts in the first 2028 AI year
Take company-paid robot repair inspection training if offered
Apply for a funded field inspection vacancy if one opens
Ask the union to require paid robot trial staffing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that full AI in 2028 can write our plans, but field robots are not due until around 2031. I would argue for a public trial log before a robot works near a live line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 for the thinking AI and 48 for the robots. The three paid years matter, but my daily use of AI does not guarantee a job once machines can handle the physical repair too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the company for paid training on inspecting robot repairs and start documenting the faults our crew catches. In the first year after 2028 I would keep line shifts, apply for any funded field inspection opening, and ask the union for a no-unpaid-trial rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel rushed but alert. The mortgage and the children make a gap in wages frightening, so I would only move to a post whose pay and field duties are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you document this week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cracked insulator at the east substation looked sound in a photograph until we got close. I would record why the camera view missed it and what a safe inspection needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no field inspection job exists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep repairing lines while the company still pays for that work and push the union to negotiate trial staffing. I would look at vacancies at the water utility too, but there are not many nearby.

say: I would seek **real repair data** before a robot is called safe.
I would separate **2031 thinking AI** from line-capable robots around 2034.
think: At **51**, I may still need a wage and cannot assume grown children or the mortgage cost nothing.
An **office safety title** may vanish if AI handles its reports.
do: Join a paid **field technology panel** and photograph faults now.
In **2031**, compare trial repairs and take funded field inspection training if it leads to a vacancy.
feel: I feel **more breathing room** and wary of training for disappearing paperwork.
S3.quote: A full thinking system could do the paperwork, so a title by itself is no protection.
fieldNote: Sara wants the panel to define **robot fault limits** using observed repairs, not promotional claims.
She questions a seemingly safe **office role** because full thinking AI could handle its paperwork before robots arrive.

steps.text: Keep paid line climbing until a field offer is signed
Join the paid field technology panel and compare robot trial faults
Take funded field safety inspection training if tied to a vacancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the five-year warning gives us room to test, but the dates still matter: thinking AI in 2031 and line-capable robots around 2034. I want repair data before anyone calls a robot safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when full AI arrives and 51 when robots arrive. My older child could be leaving school, but we may still have a mortgage, and a report-writing inspection job may disappear under AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask to sit on a paid field technology panel and keep a fault notebook with photographs. In 2031 I would compare actual repairs with robot trial results, take a funded safety inspection course if it leads to a field vacancy, and keep climbing until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more room to breathe than in the fast case. I also feel the trap: the job I train for must still need a person after AI handles reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the panel decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should set a rule for which faults a robot may attempt and when a crew must go out. I would take the cracked insulator example rather than argue from a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the company offered an office safety role, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how much is paperwork and how much is inspection at the pole. A full thinking system could do the paperwork, so a title by itself is no protection.

say: I would ask for **yearly repeat-fault reports** from robot pilots.
I would explain that **2036 AI** changes planning before robots reach repairs around 2039.
think: I will be **56** at the robot date and may still need wages for a mortgage.
A **field audit post** could use my experience if it pays for on-site judgement.
do: Keep paid **line repairs** and review annual pilot faults with the union.
After **2036**, apply for a funded field audit post and pay extra mortgage principal from reliable overtime.
feel: I feel **steadier** because I can judge evidence across the decade.
S4.quote: My children may live elsewhere by then, but that is not a pension plan, and the mortgage may still need my wage.
fieldNote: Sara sees a decade for **measured trials** and continued paid physical work, while keeping the field and office dates distinct.
Her proposed **audit move** depends on funded on-site duties, and mortgage overpayments stay small while the children have costs.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs through the first 2036 AI year
Review yearly robot pilot repeat faults with the union
Apply for a funded field audit vacancy if on-site duties remain
Pay thirty from reliable overtime toward mortgage principal when affordable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a decade can produce a real safety record if we start now. Full thinking AI by 2036 changes plans and reports; line-capable robots around 2039 change the repair itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the first date and 56 at the robot date. My children may live elsewhere by then, but that is not a pension plan, and the mortgage may still need my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep repairing lines and ask for yearly reports on repeat faults from any robot pilot. In the first year after 2036 I would review those reports with our union, apply for a funded field audit vacancy if it still uses on-site judgement, and pay extra toward the mortgage from reliable overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steadier over the next few years because the work in front of me is physical and paid. I can make decisions from trial records as they come rather than betting everything this winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an audit job rather than more climbing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know which repairs look fine from the road and fail in bad weather. If the company pays a person to check those spots in the field, my experience has a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of the extra pay would go to the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with thirty from a regular overtime payment and adjust if the household budget allows. I will not promise the whole payment while the children still need things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there are only about three years between thinking AI and robots at the line. Paid field training with a funded vacancy would help, as would a union seat at robot trials and clear results from actual repairs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the course leads to after AI writes the reports. I could learn quickly and still train for a job the company no longer pays for.

headlineQuote: I could learn quickly and still train for a job the company no longer pays for.
portrait: Sara is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
She uses **AI daily** to find records, but checks approved manuals before touching equipment.
Her **thin savings** make household bills dangerous despite confidence in her physical repair skills.
Across the scenarios she asks for **field evidence**, union oversight and funded roles that still need on-site judgement.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** leaves only three years before robots might reach her hands-on line work.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **field training**, a funded vacancy and union access to actual robot trial results would help.
